title: Could you live without a refrigerator?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore whether people can live without a refrigerator ("de-fridging"), a green-living trend popularized around 2009 by a New York Times article. They compare a fridge's electricity use to other household appliances, discuss which foods can be kept out of the fridge (butter, condiments, onions, potatoes, cilantro, avocados with a banana in a paper bag), and cooling alternatives like coolers and chest freezers with frozen water bottles. The conversation then covers food waste statistics, developing-world post-harvest losses, landfill methane, Zero Waste Home blogger Bea Johnson's "5 Rs", edible weeds, license plate siding, a debunked "poop burger" story, the London fatberg made of wet wipes, toilet paper alternatives, and an Einstein no-moving-parts refrigerator. The episode ends with a listener mail segment from a St. Louis police officer about a meth lab found in a Gatorade bottle, and a sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter and green movement
segments.summary: Hosts joke about Jerry eating broccoli stalks, then discuss how recycling has become mainstream and how some green trends seem like fads.

segments.title: Giving up refrigerators as a green trend
segments.summary: A 2009 New York Times article described people unplugging refrigerators to be greener. The hosts compare it to sterilization and note the New York Times article described a divide among eco-conscious people.

segments.title: Energy use of refrigerators versus other appliances
segments.summary: A typical post-2000 fridge uses about 450 kWh per year, less than a clothes dryer, central air, or furnace, which uses around 6,000 kWh. The hosts translate CO2 emissions into miles driven.

segments.title: Foods that don't need refrigeration
segments.summary: The hosts discuss keeping butter, condiments, onions, tomatoes, potatoes, cauliflower, cilantro, and avocados out of the fridge, along with tips for cutting onions and ripening avocados with a banana in a paper bag.

segments.title: Cooling alternatives: coolers and chest freezers
segments.summary: Without a fridge, people use coolers and small chest freezers. The article's chest freezer uses about 2 kWh per year. Some people freeze water bottles to keep a cooler cold.

segments.title: Shopping in small amounts and packaging tradeoffs
segments.summary: Buying smaller quantities reduces waste but can mean more packaging and more driving to the store, which affects the environmental benefit.

segments.title: Food waste statistics and developing-world food losses
segments.summary: Developing countries have high post-harvest food grain losses, and people in developing countries waste less food. The US spends about a billion dollars a year on food waste disposal, and food leftovers are the largest part of the waste stream by weight, about 12 percent of municipal landfills. Landfill methane is discussed as a greenhouse gas, and the hosts question why it is not captured for energy.

segments.title: Zero Waste Home and reuse of food scraps
segments.summary: Bea Johnson's Zero Waste Home blog describes her family's five Rs (refuse, reduce, reuse, recycle, rot), and reuse ideas like bread pudding and reviving wilted lettuce in ice water. The hosts discuss grocery store cosmetic waste.

segments.title: Edible weeds, license plate siding, and odd green trends
segments.summary: Hosts discuss edible weeds, shoes made from tires and jeans, houses sided with license plates, and a debunked story about a Japanese scientist making burgers from feces. They also discuss the London fatberg of wet wipes and grease and alternatives to toilet paper such as cloth diapers.

segments.title: Einstein refrigerator and fridge efficiency tips
segments.summary: The hosts discuss an absorption refrigerator with no moving parts co-developed by Einstein, and tips for an efficient fridge: clean coils yearly, keep it stocked, and avoid leaving the door open.

segments.title: Listener mail: meth lab in a Gatorade bottle
segments.summary: A St. Louis police officer writes that a woman arrested for shoplifting at a Walmart had a mobile meth lab in a Gatorade bottle in her purse, and that he has handled two meth labs, often with children present.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite mystery suggestions and mention contact methods and the website.
